Electromagnetic induction was discovered independently by Michael Faraday in England and Joseph Henry in the United States in the early 1830s. It is one of the most important discoveries in the history of science, as it made possible the large-scale generation of electricity.

When a conductor is pushed through a magnetic field, the induced current creates a force that opposes the motion of the conductor. You must do work (exert a force) to keep the conductor moving, and this work is what gets converted into electrical energy.

Lenz's law explains why generators require mechanical energy to operate — the induced current always creates a force that opposes the rotation, so an external force (from a turbine, engine, etc.) is needed to maintain the rotation.

A magnet with its north pole pointing downward is dropped into a coil of wire connected to a sensitive ammeter. Describe and explain what happens to the ammeter reading as the magnet falls through the coil.
As the north pole approaches the coil from above, the magnetic flux through the coil increases. By Faraday's law, an EMF is induced, and a current flows.

By Lenz's law, the induced current flows in a direction that opposes the change — it creates a magnetic field that repels the approaching north pole. So the top of the coil becomes a north pole. Using the right-hand grip rule, the current flows in a particular direction (say, anticlockwise when viewed from above). The ammeter deflects one way.
As the magnet passes through the centre of the coil and begins to exit from the bottom, the flux through the coil starts to decrease. The induced EMF (and current)
— now the coil tries to attract the retreating north pole, so the bottom of the coil becomes a north pole. The ammeter deflects the
As the magnet moves away from the coil, the rate of change of flux decreases, and the induced EMF gradually drops to zero.
If the magnet falls faster (accelerating under gravity), the EMF during the exit may be slightly larger than during the entry (due to higher speed), but the duration is shorter.

Define electromagnetic induction and state the conditions necessary.
Electromagnetic induction is the process of generating an EMF (and a current, if there is a complete circuit) by changing the magnetic flux through a conductor. Conditions: there must be a

in the magnetic flux linking the conductor — achieved by moving the conductor through a field, moving a magnet near a coil, changing the current in a nearby coil, or rotating a coil in a field. If nothing changes, no EMF is induced.

Describe the construction and operation of a simple AC generator.

A rectangular coil that can rotate on an axle between the poles of a permanent magnet. Slip rings (two continuous rings) are attached to the axle, one connected to each end of the coil. Stationary carbon brushes press against the slip rings and connect to the external circuit.

An external force rotates the coil in the magnetic field. As the coil rotates, the sides of the coil cut through field lines, and by Faraday's law an EMF is induced. The EMF is maximum when the coil is horizontal (parallel to field — maximum rate of cutting). The EMF is zero when the coil is vertical (perpendicular to field — momentarily not cutting lines). As the coil rotates past vertical, the direction in which the sides cut the field reverses, so the EMF reverses. This produces an
output. The slip rings allow the current to reverse naturally, giving AC.

AC is used because it can be easily and efficiently changed to different voltages using
. For long-distance power transmission, step-up transformers increase the voltage and reduce the current, which greatly reduces energy losses in the cables (

). At the destination, step-down transformers reduce the voltage to safe levels for consumers. DC cannot be transformed in this way (without first converting to AC), so it would suffer much greater transmission losses. This is the principal reason the mains supply is AC.
